### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to leverage the inherent redundancy in natural language as retrieval noise and propose prompt compression as a memory denoising method. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish the same empirical relationship between natural language redundancy and retrieval noise, nor do they propose prompt compression specifically as a denoising mechanism for retrieval systems. While several papers (e.g., [1], [2], [3], [4], [16]) discuss prompt compression, their focus is on improving inference efficiency or reducing computational cost, not on addressing retrieval noise caused by redundancy. Papers like [6], [8], [21], and [22] address query expansion or vocabulary mismatch but do not connect redundancy to retrieval noise or propose compression as a solution. Thus, the purpose is **not covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves demonstrating that natural language redundancy contributes to retrieval noise and proposing prompt compression (LLMLingua-2) as a denoising method for memory units, analyzing the impact of compression rate on recall and query-segment similarity. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [16], and [7] all discuss prompt compression methods, including coarse-to-fine compression ([1]), psycholinguistic principles ([3]), and entropy-based token removal ([16]). These methods are substantively equivalent to the proposed mechanism, as they all aim to reduce redundancy in prompts to improve retrieval or inference performance. The analysis of compression rate effects on recall and similarity is also covered by [16], which studies compression metrics and their impact on retrieval performance. Therefore, the mechanism is **covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring recall improvements (BM25/MPNet) and analyzing query-segment similarity changes after denoising. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [16], and [7] use similar evaluation designs, including recall metrics and similarity analysis for compressed prompts. For example, [16] evaluates compression methods using recall metrics and similarity measures, and [3] analyzes the impact of compression on retrieval performance. These designs are substantively equivalent, even if the specific benchmarks or datasets differ. Thus, the evaluation is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is dialogue systems and retrieval enhancement. Papers [9], [13], [20], [25], and [29] address retrieval systems, including dense passage retrieval ([9], [29]) and retrieval-enhanced tasks ([13], [20]). While the specific focus on dialogue systems may differ, the general application area of retrieval enhancement is well-covered by prior work. Therefore, the domain is **covered**.

## Purpose

The purpose is to build a complete segment-level memory system (SeCom) for long-term dialogue, verified on long-term conversation and dialogue segmentation tasks. Paper [8] introduces LOCOMO and evaluates long-term conversational memory of LLM agents. Paper [5] proposes recursive summarization for long-term dialogue memory. Paper [19] proposes a unified framework for long-term memory conversation. Paper [16] proposes CREEM for constructing long-term memory in chatbots. These papers share the objective of improving long-term dialogue memory, which is substantively equivalent to SeCom's purpose of building a superior segment-level memory system for long-term dialogue. Paper [8] specifically introduces LOCOMO for evaluating very long-term conversational memory, and papers [5], [16], [19] all target the same gap: enabling LLMs to maintain long-term dialogue memory.

## Mechanism

The mechanism combines: (1) dialogue segmentation to cut conversations into topically coherent segments, and (2) compression-based denoising of memory units, with the segmentation model learnable via LLM reflection with only 100 examples. Paper [5] uses recursive summarization (compression) for long-term memory but lacks segmentation. Paper [19] uses a pipeline with multiple stages including memory management. Paper [3]/[26] address topic segmentation of conversational datasets. Paper [4] provides supervised dialogue segmentation (SuperDialSeg). None of these combine segmentation + compression-based denoising + LLM reflection-based few-shot learning of segmentation rules as a unified mechanism. The specific combination of dialogue segmentation feeding into compression-based memory denoising, with LLM reflection for learning segmentation rules from 100 examples, is not present in any single prior paper.

## Evaluation

The evaluation uses: LOCOMO benchmark (introduced in [8]) with GPT4Score metric, Long-MT-Bench+, and dialogue segmentation benchmarks DialSeg711/TIAGE/SuperDialSeg. Paper [8] introduces LOCOMO and uses GPT4Score for evaluating long-term conversational memory — this is the same benchmark and metric family. Paper [4] introduces SuperDialSeg and evaluates on it. The evaluation design (using LOCOMO + GPT4Score for long-term dialogue memory evaluation) is directly from [8], and the segmentation evaluation on SuperDialSeg/DialSeg711 follows the design from [4] and [3]/[26]. These are named benchmarks and metric families used in prior work.

## Domain

The domain is dialogue systems / dialogue segmentation. Papers [3], [4], [6], [7], [8], [14], [19], [26] all work in dialogue systems and/or dialogue segmentation. This is clearly covered.
